Hi,

I just created this issue

https://github.com/IQSS/dataverse/issues/12437

and this PR with the proposed changes:

https://github.com/IQSS/dataverse/pull/12439

@Philip Durbin 🚀 suggested to make @Juan Pablo Tosca Villanueva aware of it, so I just did that :slight_smile:

The idea is to Make OpenAPI Great (Again) by adding currently missing annotations that provide descriptions and more context for the REST endpoints, making them more machine-actionable. My ultimate goal is to implement a Dataverse MCP server based on this improved OpenAPI documentation.
Only 2,655 lines to review in that PR. :smile:
I should back up and say I support the direction and goals! MCP! Yes!
@Balázs Pataki giving the high line count in the PR, is it fair to assume all the descriptions are AI-generated?
Also, I'm sure you realize that this PR will be prone to merge conflicts.

Almost certainly this specific PR cannot be merged. It just can't. HOWEVER. Since the changes are mostly annotations, we can keep track of what needs to be changed where, and how and carve this into say 12-15 PRs with 3-4 commits each. Within 3 months or so. This will reduce review burden and merge conflicts a lot. This is an important target for UNC, so I'm willing to stick with this and see it through. After a few PRs are merged, maybe Balázs can start prototyping the MCP server based on the improved OpenAPI spec.

Does this sound reasonable to y'all?

Yes, these are all AI generated and it is a lot, that's why I raised the issue to discuss how to cope with this. I know from experience that sometimes even 4 lines of changes can take months to get tested and approved.

I assume that the annotations are nearly all correct, though the phrasing of the descriptions may not always be. But still, if we only need to review the description texts (for methods and arguments) it is still a more manageable job then adding these annotations from scratch.

Having said that, since these changes only affect the method headings (adding annotations and some reformatting, plus some import at the beginning of the files) I don't actually expect too much merge conflicts.

I was also thinking about creating a specific review tool for going through these changes in case the github review tools are not sufficient here.

Regarding the MCP server: I already have implemented one based on FastMCP. As you will see I also added tags to the methods, which allow configuration of various "profiles" for the MCP. 580+ tools are too much and users usually don't need all of them, so DV installations could be able to filter by tags what kind of tools they want to expose via the MCP. Such profiles could be "data steward", or "read-only discovery" and then only tools supporting these use cases would be offered by the MCP. This implementation is now a separate python process that need to be run and managed, but we can also think about building a Java implementation right into DV.

Hey @Balázs Pataki what is the motivation behind getting the score back up? Looking at the PR I'm a little worried. While the score may get back up (quantitativly), it's not a qualitative improvement of our OpenAPI spec.

As the way our Java REST API endpoints responds has grown organically (one might even say out of control) towards not using DTOs, there's not a lot of schema that we can add now to the spec. On the other hand, that's one of the most essential things a client needs when using the spec to implement some action against the API.

So while the score is back up, the client will not have a lot of more information. The schema will literally say "expect a JSON object" and so on. I'm not sure this will help anyone. It's like code coverage: a high number doesn't tell you of what quality the test are made, how well they cover edge cases etc.

My vote would be to be honest and stick with a 89. It's not too bad, but looking at a 98 and then getting a lot of nothing seems contraproductive as an expectation to set and communicate.

That said: I very much fear it will be a lot of work digging ourselves out of the hole we dug... (But that's true for a lot of things gone wrong with the API architecture.)

I've invested a few tokens a while ago by asking Qwen3.8-Flash-Next to review the API Datasets class (was testing the LLM deployment on a server). A god class example par excellence with 7000 lines. Takes ~60kT / ~500MB of KV context cache to dig through. The TL;DR for a refactoring was:

  1. Split into focused resource classes (or sub-resources): DatasetResource, DatasetVersionResource, FileEmbargoResource, FileRetentionResource, GlobusTransferResource, DatasetTypeResource, CurationStatusResource, ThumbnailsResource, etc. A base AbstractDatasetResource can hold the shared findDatasetOrDie / response(…) helpers.
  2. Extract the per-file attribute logic (embargo, retention) into a shared generic helper or a small service.
  3. Standardize on one dataset-lookup pattern, one permission-check pattern, and one error-response pattern.
  4. Move handleVersion + DsVersionHandler into a package-level utility.
  5. Standardize parameter names ({id} everywhere for the dataset identifier).
  6. Reduce injected dependencies per class to only what each sub-resource needs.
  7. Break long methods into validation / orchestration / response steps.

The class is clearly functional (it's a production API for a real system), but from a maintainability and testability standpoint it is far from well-designed.

And it's not even mentioning response schemas, as the other tasks are far more important and complex... :see_no_evil: I might do this again and throw GitNexus into the mix, so the model has a better chance at understanding the Dataverse codebase context (haha).

Yes, the current fix is to explicitly declare that we return "an object", although we don't specify its shape. The regression was that it didn't even say that it was "an object" and now it does . The vacuum score is not about how nice your API is functionally (I mean, whether you return a nicely shaped object or just an opaque object type), but whether it is properly defined so that it is machine interpretable. That's why I think 98 is reasonable with our current implementation and fix.

Of course the real solution - as I also suggested in the issue - is to have proper DTO-s returned, which then SmallRye will define proper JSON schemas for and so users would know the exact shape of the returned values.

Until then I think it is a valid and honest declaration that we return "an object" or "a string" and it is still more useful and correct than saying nothing.

I went ahead and used your PR to generate an updated OpenAPI spec.
As one of the intentions for OpenAPI specs these days isn't just implementing an autogenerated client, but agentic AI usage, I went ahead and threw an agent at this.

Using Pi Agent backed with a Qwen3.8:27B model, I asked this question: "Can you please read the file target/classes/META-INF/openapi.yaml, analyze it and give me a thorough and honest overview of problems with this OpenAPI spec for a consumer (looking to implement a client or using it in an agentic AI context)? "

It took a while, installed Python openapi-schema-validator and openapi-spec-validator plus NPM-based Redocly CLI, looked at the source code and came up with a long result: https://iffmd.fz-juelich.de/81LtXoJlQniOz2FVBz1uxg
I haven't proof-read all of them yet, but some things are already standing out to me as valid things.

In the meantime I ran the same prompt in chatgpt and it gave similar result: the biggest problem being the missing response types. ("~80% of responses have no schema" in your report)

https://chatgpt.com/share/6aaa5a33-111c-83eb-8bee-c64b9050f857

1. Looking at https://demo.dataverse.org/openapi, there really is no "servers" block mixed into the "template". The missing API base URL is probably bad, too. (Verified with YAML from Demo)
  2. The error schema is a problem. @Johannes D and @Vera Clemens have already proposed adapting RFC9457 going forward, which is a good idea.
  3. The "no response schemas" part is obvious and we know that, that will be a larger endavour.
  4. The request contracts might be worth a proof read. We thought we did quite good on those, but normal validation tools can only get so far...
  5. Some of the security things look legit - we probably don't do a good job on those.
  6. We should double check the path collisions Redocly flags. That would be an easy fix.

I know that a lot of API endpoints have strange content types attached, like "/". In another run it did mention those as a potential source of problems for clients/agents as well. (Misleading what parameters should be sent, etc)

I'm not sure who's to blame here: did we do a poor job at annotating with API specs, are some of our Jersey content type annotations bad or is the generator doing a poor job. Needs further evaluation.

So, how should we proceed with knowing all this? These are mostly deep architectural/source code issues we already knew about. The current OpenAPI work just made it more visible.

Of course, where we can just fix something with OpenAPI declarations, which is relatively easy, we should do that.
Yeah, I'd favor we address anything we can address with OpenAPI specs.

That's why I added tags to semantically group functionalities, so that you can have a "datasteward" like MCP which is about search, metadatada editing, publication. Anothor one for DV sysadmins, etc.

So, in my FastAPI based MCP server I can configure "profiles" like this, based on tags in the openapi:

# Profile: Data steward
# For creating, editing, searching, publishing, and organizing datasets/files.
INCLUDE_TAGS=Datasets,Dataverses,Files,Search,Licenses,Dataset Fields,Metadata
EXCLUDE_TAGS=Admin,Users,Roles,Notifications,Workflows,External Tools,Dataverse Featured Items
That's pretty cool!
(you don't need to specify both include/exclude, this is just for an example)

So, my openapi enhancement attempts just tried to document what we have with more (human) descriptions without changing any API-s. In this respect with all these nicer description, we are of course nearly as bad with most of the input-output semantics as before.

For example, we have this endpoint:

    @POST
    @AuthRequired
    @Path("{identifier}/metadatablockfacets/isRoot")
    @Consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    @Operation(summary = "Assign metadata block facet root status",
            description = "Changes whether a dataverse is a metadata-block-facet root.")
    @RequestBody(description = "Boolean text indicating whether the dataverse is a metadata-block-facet root.")
    public Response updateMetadataBlockFacetsRoot(@Context ContainerRequestContext crc,
            @Parameter(description = "Dataverse alias, id, or persistent identifier.", required = true)
            @PathParam("identifier") String dvIdtf,
            @RequestBody(description = "Boolean text indicating whether the dataverse is a metadata-block-facet root.")
            String body) {
        try {
            final boolean blockFacetsRoot = parseBooleanOrDie(body);

These were already defined:

    @POST
    @AuthRequired
    @Path("{identifier}/metadatablockfacets/isRoot")
    @Consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)

But then in code we have 

final boolean blockFacetsRoot = parseBooleanOrDie(body);

which clearly doesn't expect a JSON as input but a true or false or similar string value.

What I want to say is that a good vacuum value do not mean a semantically correct API, but conformance to OpenAPI spec.
